title: Native LAM Reaches 93.6% Success on RoboTwin 2.0 Benchmark
summary: New Native LAM method uses one video diffusion transformer for robot learning, hitting 93.6% on RoboTwin 2.0. PAWlicy triples real-world task success rates.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Native LAM uses one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both inverse and forward dynamics model, reaching 93.6% on RoboTwin 2.0.
- PAWlicy policy lifts real-robot success from 23.3% to 76.7% on block stacking and 33.3% to 90.0% on shoe placement.
- Method compresses 3,456 video tokens into 32 latent action tokens using Kairos 3.1 backbone and learnable dynamics registers.


A new robot learning method posted to Hugging Face on November 24, 2026 achieves a 93.6% average success rate on the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark by operating a single pretrained[video diffusion transformer](https://emergent.sh/glossary/video-diffusion-model) as both inverse and forward dynamics model. The approach, called Native LAM (Latent Action Model), uses learnable dynamics registers to compress thousands of video tokens into compact latent actions that drive a 3.8B vision-language-action policy named PAWlicy.


Officially released on November 24, 2026, the paper titled 'World Models as Native Latent Action Models' represents a shift from dedicated inverse-dynamics encoders to a unified architecture that reuses existing video generation capacity. The method trains on counterfactual temporal pairs, video clips that share an identical first frame but differ only in motion, forcing the dynamics registers to encode motion information and nothing else.


## Architecture and Token Compression


Native LAM builds on the Kairos 3.1 video diffusion backbone. The pretrained transformer normally produces 3,456 video tokens of dimension 2,560 for a single clip. The new method inserts learnable dynamics registers that compress this representation into 32 latent action tokens of dimension 128. These compact tokens serve as the causal bridge between the inverse dynamics model (which infers actions from observed motion) and the forward dynamics model (which predicts future frames given actions).


The training procedure relies on counterfactual pairs: two video segments that begin from the same state but diverge in trajectory. By minimizing reconstruction error on these paired clips, the registers learn to carry only the motion delta between the two futures. The result is a latent action space that generalizes across robots, scenes, and even from human demonstrations to robot execution, with no explicit transfer objective required during training.


## Benchmark Performance


PAWlicy, the 3.8B policy trained on Native LAM's latent actions, reaches 93.6% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, the highest number reported in the paper's own comparison table. On the LARY benchmark, Native LAM outperforms existing latent-action models on both action classification and control regression tracks. The paper attributes the gains to the richer representations available in a large pretrained video diffusion model compared to smaller task-specific encoders.


RoboTwin 2.0 has drawn a cluster of submissions in recent weeks. The same day this paper appeared, a separate Tsinghua-Tencent team posted another entry under different evaluation conditions, signaling growing competition on the benchmark.


## Real-World Robot Results


On physical hardware, PAWlicy lifts the baseline π0.5 policy from 23.3% to 76.7% success on stacking three blocks and from 33.3% to 90.0% on putting shoes in a box. The deltas are large enough to suggest practical utility in unstructured tasks where precise manipulation matters. The authors also demonstrate a replay property: a latent action extracted from one robot video can be regenerated on a different robot, in a new scene, or from a human hand video, without additional fine-tuning.


## Training Data and Limitations


Native LAM trains on 46 video sources, but only two, AgiBot World 2026 and DROID, provide kinematic grounding (joint angles, end-effector positions). Everything else is vision-only. The authors acknowledge that the entire result depends on a single backbone, Kairos 3.1, and that broader validation is needed. Future work will test other video diffusion transformers, isolate the contribution of kinematic data, and evaluate geometric changes and additional robot platforms.


The reliance on one pretrained model means replication and extension will require access to comparable video generation capacity. The paper does not specify compute requirements for training the dynamics registers or for running PAWlicy inference on real robots, leaving open questions about deployment cost and latency.


## What This Means


Native LAM demonstrates that large video generation models can double as dynamics models without architectural changes, lowering the barrier to building high-performance robot policies. The 93.6% RoboTwin 2.0 result and the threefold real-world success improvements suggest the approach scales with pretraining quality. If the replay property holds across a wider set of robots and tasks, it may simplify transfer learning in manipulation. The November 24, 2026 release opens the door to follow-on work testing alternative backbones and expanding kinematic grounding beyond two datasets.
